failures.title: BMW S63B44T4 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Timing Chain Tensioner Wear - Improved but Still a Monitoring Point
items.onset: 60,000-100,000 miles (less common than early S63 but still reported)
items.whatHappens: The S63B44T4 uses a revised timing chain tensioner compared to earlier S63 variants, but the design still relies on oil pressure and a spring mechanism that can weaken over time. Cold‑start rattle is a warning sign; if ignored, chain slack can lead to timing drift and, in extreme cases, valve‑to‑piston interference. The T4 variant is more durable than the early S63B44, but tensioner wear is still the most documented mechanical failure.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early (rattle only), tensioner and guide replacement is a manageable repair (£1,500-£2,500). If the chain has jumped, the engine is typically beyond economical repair - a full replacement is the only safe option. → Read our full timing chain failure guide

items.title: Hot‑Vee Heat Stress - Valve Stem Seals & Plastic Coolant Lines
items.whatHappens: The hot‑vee layout places the turbos inside the V of the engine, generating extreme heat. Over time, this degrades valve stem seals (leading to oil consumption and blue smoke on start‑up) and makes plastic coolant lines around the turbos brittle and prone to cracking. The T4 uses improved materials over earlier S63 engines, but these issues still occur on higher‑mileage examples.
items.repairVsReplace: Valve stem seal replacement is a labour‑intensive job (£3,000-£5,000) and often done alongside other work. Coolant line replacement is cheaper but usually done at the same time. If oil consumption is excessive or the engine has overheated, a reconditioned unit may be more cost‑effective. → Read our full oil consumption guide

items.title: Turbocharger Wear - Wastegate Rattle & Bearing Play
items.whatHappens: The S63's twin‑twin‑scroll turbos are under constant high‑temperature stress. Wastegate bushings wear, causing rattle on deceleration, and turbo bearings can develop play, leading to reduced boost and oil consumption. This is more common on high‑mileage examples or cars that have been aggressively tuned.
items.repairVsReplace: Turbo refurbishment or replacement is a specialist job (£1,500-£3,000 per turbo). If both turbos are failing and the engine is out for other work, many owners opt for a full reconditioned unit with refreshed turbos already included.

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the S63B44T4
variants.intro: The S63B44T4 is the final iteration of the S63TU engine family, distinguished from earlier variants by its 625 hp output, specific turbocharger hardware, and updated engine management. It is the engine found in the F90 M5 Competition (post‑2020), M8 Competition, and competition‑spec X5M/X6M. Where the code appears: - Stamped on a metal plate on the engine block (left‑hand side, near the timing cover) - On the V5C logbook under "Engine number" (the first 8 characters will read S63B44T4) - Via BMW VIN decoder - the 7th character of the VIN indicates engine type Commonly confused with: - S63B44T0 - earlier Competition variant with 575 hp (F10 M5 Competition) - S63B44T2 - 600 hp variant (F90 M5 standard, pre‑LCI) - S63B44T3 - 600-617 hp variant (F90 M5 pre‑Competition, some M8) - S68B44 - new hybrid V8 (X5M/X6M, M5 hybrid)

relatives.description: - the earlier 600-617 hp variant found in pre‑LCI F90 M5 Competition models. The T4 increased output to 625 hp with revised turbo control and engine mapping, while retaining the same long‑block hardware.

- the new 4.4‑litre V8 with mild‑hybrid assistance, introduced in the latest X5M/X6M and the next‑generation M5. It uses a 48‑volt system and produces up to 635 hp - the T4 is the last pure ICE V8 in the high‑output M line.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement S63B44T4 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used S63B44T4 can be viable if it comes from a low‑mileage, well‑maintained car with full documented history. However, these engines are often driven hard; without proof that the timing chain tensioner has been addressed and the turbos are in good health, a used unit is a gamble. Many used S63 engines are sold with known issues. Factor in £2,000-£4,000 for preventative work (tensioner, valve stem seals) if the history is unclear. Link once: /services/used-engines

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper S63B44T4 recon is the gold standard for M5/M8/X5M/X6M owners. A quality recon should include: full strip and inspection, new timing chain tensioner and guides, refreshed valve stem seals, replacement of all plastic coolant lines, turbo refurbishment, new gaskets and seals, and a full test. With a 12-24 month warranty, this gives you a fresh engine with all known weaknesses engineered out - well worth the £10,000-£14,000 supply cost for a high‑value M‑car. Link once: /services/reconditioned-engines

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified when the original engine has suffered catastrophic failure (chain jump, seized turbos, overheating) and the car is a low‑mileage collector or cherished daily driver. An upgraded rebuild should include forged pistons, upgraded rod bearings, a reinforced timing chain guide, and a full cylinder head overhaul. This is specialist work and typically only makes sense for cars with strong residual value (£30,000+). Link once: /services/rebuilt-engines

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: All engines can be supplied and fitted through our network of vetted BMW M specialists nationwide, with 12‑month warranty on reconditioned and rebuilt units. Link once: /services/supply-and-fit
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: The S63B44T4 typically sits in F90 M5 Competition, M8, X5M and X6M - cars worth £35,000-£100,000+ depending on age and condition. With a reconditioned supply cost of £10,000-£14,000, replacement is financially viable on most examples. Even a used unit at £6,000-£10,000 is a significant spend, but the high residual values of these M‑cars make replacement a sensible investment for owners looking to keep their cars on the road.

items.answer: A used S63B44T4 can be viable if it has full documented history and proof of tensioner and turbo condition. However, these engines are often driven hard; without evidence of preventative work, a used unit carries significant risk. A reconditioned engine is the safer choice - it typically includes new tensioner, refreshed valve stem seals, replaced coolant lines, and turbo refurbishment, with a 12‑24 month warranty. → Compare used and recon prices side‑by‑side.
bullets: Used: cheaper (£6k-£10k) but factor in £2k-£4k for preventative work.

items.question: How do I confirm my car has the S63B44T4 and not another S63 variant?
items.answer: Check the engine code stamped on the block (left‑hand side near the timing cover) - it will read S63B44T4. The V5C logbook also lists the full engine number, with the first 8 characters identifying the code. → Enter your registration and we’ll verify your exact code.
bullets: Common confusions: S63B44T3 (600-617 hp), S63B44T2 (600 hp), and S63B44 (first generation).
Fitting a different TU variant requires ECU and potentially hardware changes.

items.question: How long does an S63B44T4 engine typically last?
items.answer: With meticulous maintenance and early preventative work, these engines can exceed 120,000 miles. The forged internals are robust, and the T4 benefits from the most refined TU iteration. The limiting factors are the timing chain tensioner and hot‑vee heat stress. → A reconditioned unit with these items addressed can be expected to last well beyond 100k miles.
bullets: Tensioner and guide replacement recommended at 60k-80k miles.
Strict adherence to 5,000‑mile oil changes with BMW M‑spec oil is critical.
Regular inspection of coolant lines and valve stem seals extends lifespan.
